meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When somebody says it's not about the money, it's about the money'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mencken — Kin Hubbard wrote it in dialect in his Abe Martin column on 24 November 1916. The Mencken credit traces to a January 1999 Senate speech.

answer.label: Not H. L. Mencken — actually Kin Hubbard
answer.authorDates: 1868–1930 · American cartoonist and humorist · creator of Abe Martin
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying to Kin Hubbard’s syndicated Abe Martin feature, printed in the Franklin Evening News of 24 November 1916 in dialect: “When a feller says: ‘It hain’t th’ money, but th’ principle o’ th’ thing,’ it’s th’ money.” The smooth modern one-liner is a much later rewording, and no Mencken book, column or letter has ever been produced for it — QI mentions Mencken only as an incorrect credit given by Senator Dale Bumpers in January 1999.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: New Sayings By Abe Martin; and Velma’s Vow
“Abe Martin” syndicated column, Franklin Evening News (Franklin, PA), 24 November 1916

source.excerpt: When a feller says: ‘It hain’t th’ money, but th’ principle o’ th’ thing,’ it’s th’ money.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ names the earliest documented instance: Kin Hubbard’s syndicated Abe Martin feature in the Franklin Evening News of 24 November 1916, reading “When a feller says: ‘It hain’t th’ money, but th’ principle o’ th’ thing,’ it’s th’ money.” QI notes it appeared the same year in Hubbard’s book New Sayings by Abe Martin and Velma’s Vow.

Wikiquote’s sourced Hubbard page ↗ carries the saying as “When a fellow says, ‘It hain’t the money, but th’ principle o’ the thing,’ it’s th’ money,” cited to Hoss Sense and Nonsense (1926), with a modernised variant from Clifton Fadiman’s The American Treasury, 1455–1955, p. 993.

Per QI, the centennial edition of John Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations credited Hubbard with the line, citing his 1926 collection — so the correct attribution was in the standard reference work long before the internet reassigned it. Quote Investigator ↗

The Mencken credit has a traceable point of entry. In January 1999, arguing against President Clinton’s conviction, Senator Dale Bumpers told the Senate: “H.L. Mencken said one time, ‘When you hear somebody say, this is not about money — it’s about money.’” Fox News ↗
source.excerptNote: This dialect version is the wording Quote Investigator documents as the earliest instance. The familiar modern sentence — “When somebody says it’s not about the money, it’s about the money” — is a later smoothing with no identified author, not anything Hubbard or Mencken is recorded as writing.

sourceLink.text: New Sayings By Abe Martin (c. 1916), free scan listed at The Online Books Page

source.rightsNote: Hubbard’s documented wording was first published in a newspaper column on 24 November 1916 and collected in books of 1916 and 1926 — all well before 1931, so the text shown here is in the public domain in the United States. Hubbard himself died in 1930. The polished modern paraphrase circulating under Mencken’s name has no identified author or first publication, so no rights claim is made for that specific wording.

author.name: Kin Hubbard
author.heading: The man who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1868–1930 · American cartoonist, humorist and journalist · creator of Abe Martin
author.bio: Frank McKinney “Kin” Hubbard was an Indianapolis cartoonist and humorist whose creation Abe Martin — a lean, hat-wearing philosopher from fictional Bloom Center in Brown County, Indiana — ran in The Indianapolis News from 17 December 1904, six days a week for twenty-six years. Each drawing carried a one-sentence crack in rural dialect, and the best of them outlived the cartoon entirely. Hubbard’s specialty was exactly this kind of deflating observation about what people claim to be arguing about versus what they are actually arguing about.

cite.sourceCitation: Kin Hubbard, “Abe Martin,” Franklin Evening News (Franklin, PA), November 24, 1916 — earliest documented instance per Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: When They Say It’s Not About Money, It’s About Money,” August 29, 2020. Collected the same year in New Sayings by Abe Martin; and Velma’s Vow (Indianapolis: Abe Martin Pub. Co., c. 1916), and later in Abe Martin: Hoss Sense and Nonsense (1926).

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a proverb with a documented author who almost never gets named. The polished modern wording circulated unattributed for years, and then collected famous owners.

items.why: The Quote Investigator survey ↗ of this saying mentions Mencken exactly once — as an incorrect credit given by U.S. Senator Dale Bumpers in January 1999, during President Clinton’s Senate impeachment trial. Fox News transcribes the moment ↗: “H.L. Mencken said one time, ‘When you hear somebody say, this is not about money — it’s about money.’” QI does not validate the attribution, and no Mencken book, essay, column or letter has been produced for it.

Goodreads ↗ prints the line under Mencken’s name with no book or date attached, above its own disclaimer that quotes are community-added and unverified; AZQuotes ↗ does the same with no source at all. Neither offers anything a reader could check.

items.who: George Young, and one commentator's grandfather
items.why: Before Mencken got it, the saying was being handed to whoever had said it most recently. QI’s timeline ↗ records columnist Mike Lupica crediting football executive George Young in August 1995, and Shannon Sharpe crediting his grandfather in December 1999 — the classic signature of a proverb whose real author has been forgotten.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Kin Hubbard’s, first documented in his Abe Martin column of 24 November 1916 and credited to him in Bartlett’s as early as the 1955 centennial edition — Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: How a dialect gag became a Mencken aphorism
lead: Hubbard’s original is written the way Abe Martin talked: “When a feller says: ‘It hain’t th’ money, but th’ principle o’ th’ thing,’ it’s th’ money.” The joke is not about money at all — it is about the gap between the reason people give and the reason they have. That is a durable enough observation that it survived being stripped of every apostrophe Hubbard put in it.

By the 1990s the dialect was gone and the saying was floating free. Quote Investigator’s timeline ↗ picks it up in sports commentary — tennis player Jim Courier in March 1995, and columnist Mike Lupica crediting football executive George Young in August 1995 — and then in January 1999 Senator Dale Bumpers put it on the Senate floor with Mencken’s name on it. An unattributed proverb plus a famous cynic is a stable compound; it has stayed attached ever since.
context.detailsSummary: The reference books got it right before the internet got it wrong
detailsBody: The line was not obscure. Per Quote Investigator ↗, the 1955 centennial edition of John Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations credited Hubbard, citing his 1926 collection Hoss Sense and Nonsense. Wikiquote ↗ also records a modernised rendering — “When a fellow says, ‘It ain’t the money but the principle of the thing,’ it’s the money” — in Clifton Fadiman’s The American Treasury, 1455–1955, p. 993. The smoothing-out of the dialect was already under way in print, decades before anyone thought to hand the line to Mencken.
context.pull: “It hain’t th’ money, but th’ principle o’ th’ thing” — it’s th’ money.
